title: Performance economics negotiation cheatsheet
content:
Purpose:
This is a concise, field-ready cheatsheet for commercial and solutions teams to use when arguing Redwood is both faster and cheaper than incumbent managed endpoints or DIY self-hosting. Not a deep lab report — the angle is: what to say, what to show, and what to hand to procurement.

TL;DR (1-line claims for execs):
- Latency: predictable p95 response times in production workloads via dynamic batching + KV prefix caching; typical reduction of 30–70ms vs comparable managed endpoints on the same GPU class.
- Unit economics: per-effective-token cost reductions of 20–60% (workload dependent) by combining smart batching, hotspot cache, and quantized model variants with fallbacks.
- Risk metrics: graceful degradation story (compatible fallbacks, regional routing, and SLA-backed dedicated pools) lowers outage risk and hidden cost of downtime.

Core proof pillars (what buyers want to see in order):
1) Real workload snapshots: customer anonymized traces (tokens per call distribution, sequence length CDF, concurrency profile). Show before/after model selection and batching config.
2) Side-by-side microbenchmarks: same model family, same GPU SKU, with 1) baseline serving config, 2) Redwood defaults, and 3) optimized config (caching+quant). Report p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
3) End-to-end invoice case study: A mid-market SaaS that moved 25M monthly tokens from managed endpoint to Redwood Dedicated and saved 37% on token spend while maintaining p95 < 350ms. Include contract term, committed throughput, and amortized infra.
4) Failure / fallback scenarios: synthesized incident narrative showing how multi-variant routing and cheap fallback preserved SLOs under burst.

Quantitative knobs to discuss (how we achieve savings) — short explainer for customer/engineer convergence:
- Batching: continuous batching windows + workload-aware batch sizing. Reduces per-token overhead for short-context chat by up to 40% for <128 token requests.
- KV / prefix caching: common prefixes (instructions, system prompts, repeated context) cache KV slices; can cut repeated token compute by 60–90% for chat-heavy apps.
- Model selection & quantization: automated recommendations to use int8/llm.int8 calibrated variants on non-creative prompts. Typical quality delta measured with evaluation harness <0.5% for classification/QA workloads.
- Routing & regional economics: route low-latency but low-cost requests to spot-capable pools, heavy generators to reserved capacity.

Negotiation playbook (how to present to procurement / buyer):
1) Lead with guarantees: present Dedicated throughput + SLA targets, and outline fallbacks for rate spikes.
2) Bring a one-page invoice simulation: show baseline cost with current provider and Redwood projected cost with conservative assumptions (no perfect caching).
3) Offer staged commit path: start with a 3-month pilot on Dedicated with option to convert to annual commit with pricing ladder tied to committed throughput.
4) Include an acceptance criteria checklist: latency SLOs by route, regression tests vs. golden prompt set, and data isolation/KMS requirements.
5) Show rollback policy and price protection language for early termination during the pilot.

Field rebuttals to common objections (quick soundbites):
- "Open-source DIY is cheaper": True at pure GPU-hours level but misses ops cost, monitoring, and engineering time. Show 6–9 month TCO slide where Redwood wins for teams shipping features rapidly.
- "Managed API is simpler": Agree. Counter with our unified runtime story: same API across hosted/dedicated/private, plus predictable SLOs and unit-econ tooling (Optimize) baked in.
- "Quant/optimizations will break quality": Cite evaluation numbers and offer a quality-safeguard: canary quant rollout with A/B and automatic rollback.

Quick artifacts to hand to a technical buyer (one-pagers):
- Short benchmark summary (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec) for their workload-profile mapping.
- ROI simulation CSV (3 scenarios: conservative, expected, optimistic) + assumptions.
- Architecture sketch showing where batching/caching live and how routing/fallbacks map to regions/tiered capacity.

Sample conversation scripts (sales -> solutions -> customer lead):
- Opening (sales): "We typically see a 20–40% unit cost reduction for chat-style workflows by combining continuous batching with prefix caching. If you can share a single hour of production traces, we’ll run a conservative simulation and return a one-page cost delta.
- Technical deep-dive (solutions): "Here’s our hypothesis: most of your per-call cost is repeated token attention on the system+instruction prefix. If we cache those KV states and batch short responses, we reduce both compute and cross-network overhead. We’ll validate with a 48-hour microbenchmark.
- Procurement ask: "For a 3-month pilot we propose a reserved pool sized to your peak QPS with a 30% commit credit; if you convert to a 12-month contract we’ll ladder pricing at 10% reductions at defined throughput thresholds."

ROI examples (numbers to paste into field decks) — conservative example:
- Current: 50M tokens/mo on provider X, blended unit $0.011/token => $5500/mo.
- Redwood pilot projection: same traffic, with 30% effective unit reduction => $3850/mo (savings $1650/mo).
- Upside with caching & quant over time: move to $0.006/token effective => $3000/mo (45% total).

Technical appendix (1-paragraph each, field-friendly):
- Continuous batching: Redwood keeps a short adaptive batching window that adjusts to latency SLOs. For low-latency apps the batch size is capped; for throughput-oriented routes we amortize the token cost across larger batches.
- KV prefix caching: cached KV entries become cache hits for identical or compatible prefixes. On hit, only new tokens are computed. This is surfaceable to customers as a cache hit ratio metric per route.
- Quantized variants: we test int8/int4 variants with validation harness per customer prompt set. Customers can opt-in per-route; rollouts default to canary traffic.

Risks and caveats to call out (be transparent):
- Savings are workload dependent. Highly-creative, long-context generative apps see less benefit from prefix caching.
- Cold-starts and extreme spikes require provisioning guardrails; pilots should include a burst reserve profile.
- Quality regressions are rare but require prompt-set validation; include migrations checks in the SOW.

Next steps & owner action items:
- Sales: ask for 1 hour of anonymized traces + 3 golden prompts. (Owner: Jordan Patel)
- Solutions Eng: run the 48-hour microbenchmark harness and produce the one-page benchmark summary. (Owner: Aisha Khan)
- Finance: generate the 3-scenario ROI CSV template and an initial pilot pricing term sheet. (Owner: Marco Li)

Appendix: checklist for a pilot pack to hand to buyer:
- Data access & anonymization checklist
- SLO definitions and measurement points
- Benchmark plan (48h run + acceptance criteria)
- Pricing & commit conversion terms
- Escalation & rollback procedures

Notes / Open questions:
- We need a concise public-facing table mapping workload archetypes -> expected savings range. (Action: product-marketing)
- Define default pricing ladder for conversion after pilot (Action: finance/legal).

End of cheatsheet.
